difficultyReason: The paradox involves interacting mechanisms: a drug reduces average hospital stays yet total bed-days occupied by that patient population increase. Resolution requires understanding that the drug enables survival of previously fatal cases, expanding the treated population — a compound demographic-plus-policy interaction that most test-takers miss.
stimulus: A new antibiotic reduces the average length of hospital stay for patients with drug-resistant infections from 18 days to 11 days. Yet in the three years since the antibiotic was introduced, the total number of hospital bed-days consumed annually by patients with drug-resistant infections has increased by nearly 40 percent.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The antibiotic is significantly more expensive than the treatments it replaced, increasing the overall cost of care for each patient.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hospitals in several regions adopted infection-control protocols at the same time the antibiotic was introduced.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The antibiotic successfully treats infections that previously killed patients within days of hospitalization, resulting in a much larger number of surviving patients who require extended care.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Drug-resistant infections are more common in patients who have already been hospitalized for other conditions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Physicians have begun prescribing the antibiotic for a broader range of infections than those for which it was initially approved.

explanations.correct: If the antibiotic saves patients who previously died within days, those survivors now complete full treatment courses. The treated population grows dramatically, so even though each stay is shorter, the total bed-days rise — both halves of the paradox are dissolved.
explanations.A: Higher cost per patient explains a financial puzzle, not the bed-days discrepancy. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: Infection-control protocols would reduce new cases, which would decrease total bed-days — this deepens rather than resolves the paradox.
explanations.C: Correct. Population expansion (new survivors) fully accounts for the rise in aggregate bed-days despite shorter individual stays.
explanations.D: Pre-existing hospitalization status is a background fact about the patient mix; it does not explain why total bed-days rose after the drug's introduction.
explanations.E: Broader prescribing could increase patient numbers, but 'broader range of infections' is too vague — it doesn't explain why the increase is 40% while stays fell 39%, and it fails to connect the two halves causally the way C does.

difficultyReason: The paradox pairs an economic statistic (median household income rose) with a social outcome (poverty rate rose), requiring test-takers to recognize that median and rate statistics can diverge when income distribution shifts — a subtle measurement-artifact resolution most test-takers conflate with 'inequality' distractors.
stimulus: In Northvale County, median household income increased by 12 percent over the past decade, after adjusting for inflation. Yet over the same period, the percentage of households living below the federal poverty line increased from 11 percent to 16 percent.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The federal poverty line threshold has not been meaningfully updated to reflect modern living costs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A large influx of very high-income households into Northvale County raised the median while leaving the lower portion of the income distribution largely unchanged.

choices.label: C
choices.text: County residents increasingly rely on two-income households to maintain their standard of living.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Northvale County's total population grew substantially over the decade, primarily through immigration.

choices.label: E
choices.text: State tax policy changes reduced take-home pay for middle-income earners in Northvale County.

explanations.correct: If wealthy newcomers pulled the median upward without improving incomes at the bottom, the median rises while the share of households below the poverty line also rises. This demographic shift explains both statistics simultaneously — a classic measurement-artifact resolution.
explanations.A: An outdated poverty threshold would, if anything, undercount poverty, making a rise in the measured rate harder to explain, not easier. This deepens the paradox.
explanations.B: Correct. High-income in-migration skews the median upward while the lower tail of the distribution is unaffected or worsened, reconciling both data points.
explanations.C: Two-income reliance describes a coping mechanism but doesn't explain why poverty rates rose alongside the median. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: Population growth through immigration could increase the number of low-income residents, but without specifying that immigrants are disproportionately low-income, this answer is too vague to dissolve the paradox.
explanations.E: Reduced take-home pay for middle earners would likely lower the median as well, making the rising median harder to explain. This deepens the paradox.

difficultyReason: The paradox involves a policy outcome in environmental science: a city's total carbon emissions fell after a congestion tax, yet air quality in the city center worsened. Distractors address one horn each; the correct answer requires recognizing a spatial-redistribution mechanism.
stimulus: After Millford City introduced a congestion tax on vehicles entering the city center, traffic volume in that area fell by 22 percent and the city's total vehicular carbon emissions declined measurably. However, air quality monitors in the city center recorded higher concentrations of particulate matter in the two years following the tax than in the two years before it.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most help to explain the surprising phenomenon described above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Revenue from the congestion tax was used to subsidize electric-vehicle purchases by city residents.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The congestion tax exempted delivery trucks, which tend to produce higher particulate emissions per mile than private vehicles.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Drivers who avoided the city center began using older, poorly maintained vehicles on peripheral routes, increasing emissions in residential neighborhoods.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The city center's remaining vehicles, now traveling at higher speeds on less congested roads, burn fuel more efficiently, reducing their individual emissions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Construction of a new transit hub in the city center during the same period generated substantial dust and particulate matter.

explanations.correct: Construction of a transit hub would introduce a large independent source of particulate matter in the city center, explaining why local air quality worsened even as overall vehicle emissions fell. Both horns of the paradox are dissolved by this concurrent confounding event.
explanations.A: EV subsidies would reduce emissions further, which deepens the puzzle of why city-center air quality worsened.
explanations.B: Exempting delivery trucks explains some continued emissions but cannot explain why particulate levels were higher after the tax than before, since delivery traffic presumably existed before the tax as well.
explanations.C: Peripheral emissions worsening is a geographic shift, not a city-center phenomenon — this resolves neither horn within the city center and actually deepens the city-center paradox.
explanations.D: More efficient fuel burn by remaining vehicles would improve air quality, deepening rather than resolving the paradox.
explanations.E: Correct. An independent particulate source (construction) in the city center accounts for the local air-quality decline despite the citywide emissions reduction.

difficultyReason: The paradox involves law and policy: mandatory sentencing guidelines increased average sentences for drug offenses, yet the prison population for drug offenders declined. This counter-intuitive result requires a compound explanation involving prosecutorial behavior — a hidden behavioral-response mechanism.
stimulus: After a state enacted mandatory minimum sentencing guidelines for drug offenses, the average prison sentence imposed on convicted drug offenders increased from 2.4 years to 4.1 years. Nonetheless, within five years of the guidelines taking effect, the total number of inmates serving time for drug offenses in that state's prisons had fallen by 18 percent.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mandatory minimum sentences are widely regarded by legal scholars as an ineffective deterrent to drug crimes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prosecutors in the state dramatically increased their use of plea agreements that reduce charges to non-drug offenses in order to avoid triggering the mandatory minimums.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The state simultaneously expanded drug-treatment diversion programs available to first-time offenders.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Federal courts began handling an increasing share of drug prosecutions in that state after the guidelines were enacted.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prison overcrowding led officials to release some drug offenders early under a compassionate-release provision.

explanations.correct: If prosecutors systematically reduced charges to avoid mandatory minimums, far fewer defendants would be convicted of drug offenses at all. Sentences for those convicted would be longer (consistent with the data), but the number entering prison on drug charges would drop sharply — explaining the declining inmate population despite harsher sentences.
explanations.A: Whether mandatory minimums deter crime is a normative assessment; it doesn't explain the mechanical paradox of longer sentences coexisting with fewer inmates.
explanations.B: Correct. Charge reduction deflects convictions away from drug-offense categories, simultaneously explaining both the longer average sentences (only the most serious cases proceed) and the smaller drug-inmate population.
explanations.C: Diversion programs could reduce the number of convictions, partially addressing the second horn, but they don't explain why average sentence length increased. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: Federal handling of more cases would reduce state drug-offense convictions, but it doesn't explain why average sentences rose. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.E: Early release would lower the current inmate count but does not explain why the total population sentenced fell, nor why average sentence length rose.

difficultyReason: The technology paradox — a company's servers consume less energy per computation yet its total energy bill is higher — requires recognizing Jevons paradox (efficiency gains induce greater usage), a non-obvious economic principle layered with a computational-demand interaction.
stimulus: A major data company upgraded its server infrastructure so that each server now consumes 30 percent less electricity per unit of computation than before the upgrade. Yet the company's total monthly electricity expenditure is 25 percent higher than it was prior to the infrastructure upgrade.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Electricity rates in the region where the company's data centers are located increased by approximately 8 percent following the upgrade.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The upgraded servers require more skilled technicians to maintain, increasing the company's overall operating costs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The lower cost per computation enabled the company to offer cheaper services, attracting far more customers and causing the total volume of computations performed each month to more than double.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some of the old servers were retained as backup systems and continue to draw a small amount of electricity on standby.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The new servers require a more powerful cooling system, which itself consumes substantial electricity.

explanations.correct: If efficiency gains lowered the cost per computation sufficiently to more than double total computation volume, total electricity consumption would rise even though each unit of work is cheaper — a textbook Jevons paradox resolution. Both the efficiency gain and the higher total bill are explained.
explanations.A: An 8% rate increase alone cannot account for a 25% rise in expenditure if efficiency improved by 30%; the numbers don't close the gap. This is a partial, arithmetic-inconsistent resolution.
explanations.B: Technician costs affect labor expenditure, not electricity expenditure. Irrelevant to the discrepancy.
explanations.C: Correct. Doubling-plus computation volume overwhelms the 30% per-unit efficiency gain, explaining the net 25% rise in electricity costs.
explanations.D: Standby power for old backup servers would add a modest increment but cannot plausibly account for a 25% increase in total electricity expenditure. Resolves one horn only, insufficiently.
explanations.E: Enhanced cooling adds electricity demand. However, this is typically factored into server-efficiency measurements; without ruling that out, this answer is weaker than C, and it doesn't explain why the increase is specifically tied to higher usage volume.

difficultyReason: The paradox involves linguistics and historical policy: a regional language that received official government recognition and funding saw its number of fluent native speakers decline more rapidly after recognition than before. Distractors include a plausible 'prestige effect' wrong answer and a deepens-the-paradox choice.
stimulus: A regional language spoken in an isolated highland community had been losing fluent native speakers at a rate of roughly 3 percent per year for two decades. After the national government granted the language official recognition and funded immersive school programs, the rate of fluency loss accelerated to nearly 8 percent per year over the following decade.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most help to explain the surprising phenomenon described above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Official recognition increased the language's prestige, motivating more young people to study it formally.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The school programs taught a standardized written form of the language that differed significantly from the spoken vernacular, causing community elders — the primary fluent speakers — to disengage from transmission and stop teaching the language at home.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Government funding for the language programs was insufficient to cover the cost of training qualified teachers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several neighboring communities that spoke related dialects also began losing speakers at higher rates after the recognition decree.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The highland community experienced significant economic growth following official recognition, which reduced emigration of working-age residents.

explanations.correct: If the standardized school form diverged from the vernacular, elders — who were the living transmission source — felt alienated and withdrew from informal home teaching. The school programs thus replaced organic intergenerational transmission with an inferior formal substitute, accelerating net fluency loss. Both the existence of programs and the worsened decline are explained.
explanations.A: Increased prestige and formal study would predict slower decline, not faster. This deepens the paradox rather than resolving it.
explanations.B: Correct. Displacement of home transmission by an alienating standardized form is a documented mechanism in language endangerment; it simultaneously accounts for program existence and accelerated decline.
explanations.C: Underfunding would make the programs ineffective but cannot on its own explain acceleration beyond the pre-recognition baseline rate. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: Neighboring dialect communities declining faster is a separate phenomenon and does not explain the acceleration in the target community. Irrelevant.
explanations.E: Reduced emigration would keep more working-age speakers in the community, which would predict slower decline, not faster. This deepens the paradox.

difficultyReason: The paradox pairs an arts-funding outcome with an audience statistic: a city tripled arts subsidies and professional theater companies multiplied, yet average per-performance audience size fell sharply. Multiple plausible distractors target one horn; the correct answer invokes a market-saturation mechanism requiring test-takers to synthesize supply-demand reasoning with audience-behavior data.
stimulus: Over a ten-year period, a city tripled its annual arts subsidies, and the number of professional theater companies operating in the city increased from 8 to 27. However, over the same period, the average audience size per performance across all city theaters fell from 310 patrons to 190 patrons.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several of the new theater companies specialize in experimental works that appeal to smaller, niche audiences.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The total number of performances staged annually in the city increased by more than 200 percent, while the total number of theatergoers grew by only about 30 percent — meaning the same audience pool was spread across far more performances.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Theater ticket prices rose an average of 20 percent over the decade due to increased production costs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The city's population declined slightly over the ten-year period as residents relocated to suburban areas.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Arts subsidies were distributed unevenly, with the largest established companies receiving the majority of funding.

explanations.correct: If the number of performances more than tripled while the audience pool grew only 30%, simple division yields a dramatic fall in average per-performance attendance — exactly as observed. The growth in companies (and thus performances) is directly caused by the subsidies, and the per-performance decline follows arithmetically. Both horns are resolved.
explanations.A: Niche experimental audiences explain why some new companies draw fewer patrons, but this addresses only part of the average-decline horn and doesn't explain why the original eight companies would also see declining averages. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: Correct. A 200%-plus supply increase against a 30% demand increase mathematically produces the observed per-performance decline while fully accounting for the subsidy-driven company growth.
explanations.C: Higher ticket prices would reduce demand and lower attendance, but this doesn't explain why companies multiplied. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: A slight population decline could modestly reduce theatergoers, but it cannot account for a drop from 310 to 190 patrons per performance when the total audience grew. This is an opposite-direction distractor for the audience-size horn.
explanations.E: Uneven distribution of subsidies would predict that large companies thrived while small ones struggled — not that 19 new companies emerged. This actually deepens the proliferation half of the paradox.

difficultyReason: The paradox involves history and policy: a wartime rationing program reduced per-capita caloric consumption by 20 percent, yet population-level malnutrition rates fell during the same period. The resolution requires recognizing that pre-rationing inequality meant most calories went to the wealthy, so rationing redistributed intake upward for the previously under-fed majority — a distributional-equity mechanism test-takers often overlook.
stimulus: During a prolonged wartime rationing program, average per-capita caloric consumption in the affected country fell by 20 percent compared to pre-war levels. Yet rates of malnutrition-related illness in that country's hospitals declined steadily throughout the rationing period.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Wartime governments typically invest heavily in public health infrastructure, which reduces hospital admission rates independent of nutritional status.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Before rationing was introduced, food distribution was highly unequal: a small wealthy minority consumed far more than adequate nutrition while a large portion of the population consumed far less, and rationing reallocated food to the previously under-fed majority.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The rationing program also restricted the consumption of sugar and alcohol, which can contribute to certain nutritional deficiencies when consumed in excess.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many residents in rural areas were exempt from rationing because they could produce their own food, maintaining their pre-war caloric intake.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wartime labor demands caused many previously sedentary workers to take on physically demanding jobs, increasing their caloric needs substantially.

explanations.correct: If pre-rationing food distribution was grossly unequal, the overall average concealed widespread under-nutrition among the majority. Rationing compressed consumption — reducing excess at the top and increasing sufficiency at the bottom — so even though the mean fell, the share of the population with adequate nutrition rose, explaining fewer malnutrition cases. Both statistical facts are reconciled.
explanations.A: Improved public-health infrastructure could reduce hospital admissions for many reasons, but it doesn't explain why malnutrition-specific illness declined while calories fell. Resolves one horn only, and weakly.
explanations.B: Correct. A distributional reallocation from over-fed elites to the under-fed majority explains how average calories can fall while population health on the malnutrition dimension improves.
explanations.C: Reduced sugar and alcohol could improve some nutritional markers, but this is a secondary mechanism that doesn't address the core paradox of fewer total calories yet less malnutrition. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: Rural exemptions would mean rural caloric intake was unchanged, but this actually makes the average-calorie decline harder to account for and does nothing to explain improved urban malnutrition rates. Deepens one horn.
explanations.E: Greater caloric needs from physical labor would predict more malnutrition under reduced caloric availability, not less. This deepens the paradox.
